n38e56889e69e: Strong coupling between collective excitations provides a route to controlling quantum states of matter, yet its evolution under thermal fluctuations remains poorly understood. We observe a pronounced avoided crossing between magnon and phonon modes across a wide range of temperatures and find that the coupling strength remains remarkably robust with increasing temperatures. The zero-field magnon-phonon detuning decreases progressively with warming, driving the system toward resonance and thereby enhancing their hybridization near the transition temperature. This anomalous thermal evolution provides the crucial key to understanding the unusual terahertz-driven states recently reported in FePS3. More broadly, our results highlight van der Waals magnets as a promising platform for strong coupling among collective excitations and for controlling magnetic states through light-matter interactions.
n1a90f8ad5378: We investigate the geometric phase acquired by low-energy quasiparticles encircling defects in graphene. Following Anandan, this phase is the holonomy of the Poincare connection; its translational part couples momentum to torsion, giving $P_a\int T^a$. In the Katanaev-Volovich theory, dislocation torsion is confined to the defect core. For graphene, the relevant momentum is $\hbar(τ_3\KK+\mathbf q)$. We show that an isolated dislocation yields a topological valley factor $e^{\mp2πi/3}$ when its Burgers vector $\bb$ lies outside the $\sqrt3\times\sqrt3$ superlattice, together with a dispersive factor $e^{-i\mathbf q\cdot\bb}$ for every nonzero $\bb$. The topological factor recovers the lattice result of Mesaros et al. as a torsion-flux phase; 4-8 dislocations retain only the dispersive contribution. Composing Volterra elements gives the holonomy of defect complexes. At zero net Frank angle, it depends only on the net Burgers vector. The valley flux obeys a three-coloring rule: pentagons and heptagons contribute according to their Kekule site color, whereas squares and octagons do not. Atomic models confirm that ring content alone does not fix the phase: a 5-8-5 core is invisible as a divacancy or as a dislocation with $|\bb|=\sqrt3a$, but carries flux $\pm1/3$ for $\bb=2\mathbf a_1$. The torsion trace produces no geometric phase: its vector coupling violates time-reversal symmetry, while the allowed axial coupling causes only anisotropic short-range scattering.
n27de44d73734: Neutron scattering is a central probe of quantum materials, yet what quantum information can, in principle, be extracted from a scattering experiment remains unclear. Here we formulate neutron scattering as a quantum measurement, with the scattering amplitudes acting as Kraus operators on the material state. This provides a unified description of conventional intensity, coherent scattering, interferometric measurements, and entanglement witnesses, including those based on quantum Fisher information. We then ask how far this connection can be extended to nonlinear properties of a quantum state. For two independently prepared samples, we derive the general structure of probe-mediated measurement probabilities and show that, for spin-projection-conserving dynamics, low-order scattering cannot resolve certain many-body coherences required to determine purity. Conversely, an idealized single-spin protocol shows how probe-mediated exchange can access purity when the appropriate two-copy operation is realized. Our results establish a quantum-information description of neutron scattering and delineate the information accessible through conventional and interferometric measurements.
n9c7977aea7bc: The Yb delafossites NaYbSe$_2$, KYbSe$_2$, CsYbSe$_2$ and NaYbO$_2$ are candidates for the U(1) Dirac spin liquid (DSL) of the triangular lattice. Strong spin-orbit coupling gives their exchange an XXZ anisotropy $Δ$ and bond-dependent couplings $J_{\pm\pm}$, $J_{z\pm}$ that lock the spin frame to the lattice. We show that, within a single layer of a stable Heisenberg DSL, these couplings generate no relevant Lorentz-scalar operator of their own. Inversion at the bond centers removes the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya channel that gaps the kagome DSL, so the locked symmetry forbids a mass, density or current at any order and, assuming continuity, any new monopole term through charge three. Every Lorentz-scalar four-fermion operator induced by spin-orbit coupling shares an SU(4) multiplet, and hence its scaling dimension, with a Heisenberg-allowed one, and the nine non-scalar quartics without such a partner arise only at second order and are irrelevant at large $N$. The Heisenberg DSL itself allows a Lorentz-vector quartic of large-$N$ dimension 2.92, which a stable phase must also render irrelevant. Beyond a single layer, spin-orbit coupling opens an interlayer monopole channel in rhombohedral stacking. If the Heisenberg DSL is instead multicritical, an anisotropy as small as that of KYbSe$_2$ matters only below tens of mK. At the transition to 120$^\circ$ order the anisotropy is relevant, and exact diagonalization indicates that easy-plane anisotropy selects the chiral-Ising class. Existing KYbSe$_2$ neutron data below $J$ do not yet fix the K-point exponent, and gapless out-of-plane spin fluctuations at the K point would test the chiral-Ising selection.
n3e1e60202f65: Heat transport in solids is usually described in a phenomenological way via Fourier's law. However, at small time and length scales in low thermal conductivity materials, a microscopic description is needed. This is traditionally done by invoking the phonon Boltzmann Transport Equation (BTE), which has been successful in describing transport in high thermal conductivity materials. Recently, a generalization of the BTE, the Wigner Transport Equation, was developed to be able to microscopically describe transport in low thermal conductivity materials by taking into account not only phonon scattering processes but also phonon tunneling processes, so-called coherences. We present a Python package that solves the Wigner Transport Equation (WTE) in spatial and temporal Fourier space for arbitrary source terms, thereby enabling the study of heat transport at small space and time scales. This allows one to compute both static and dynamic thermal conductivities from bulk to nanoscale. Beyond that, it can be used to study the response of phonon systems in materials to arbitrary heat sources.
nd3b6a1faeafe: The ability of mechanical systems to perform basic computations has gained traction in recent years, providing a robust supplement to digital computing in off-grid, low-power, and extreme environments where electronics are inaccessible or risk failure. However, prior work has focused on Boolean logic applied via bistable structures, snap-through mechanisms, or origami lattices. Digital signal processing (DSP) underpins a wide range of computational tasks, providing the foundation for information encoding, manipulation, and analysis. In contrast to conventional DSP approaches, we present a new paradigm for analog information processing, where an elastic substrate houses a spatial wave-based platform for mechanical signal manipulation in the temporal domain. The proposed metasurface-based system exploits temperature-dependent phase transitions of shape memory alloys (SMAs) to realize key signal-processing functionalities, including gating, retention, and programmable delay of impinging mechanical loads. In doing so, we address a new set of challenges by manipulating transient mechanical waves through dispersive and lossy media. Building on this capability, we introduce the concept of mechanical wave-based memory, in which a locally resonant metamaterial's dispersion characteristics are actively reconfigured to achieve programmable delays while preserving spatial waveform integrity, and demonstrate its utility in the context of input shaping and frequency demultiplexing of superimposed waves. More broadly, the modular and scalable nature of the demonstrated framework paves the way for advanced mechanical computing architectures, enabling higher-order operations such as signal classification, parallel processing, and reservoir computing through the controlled sequencing and temporal alignment of mechanical signals.
n6d5d214ff942: Quantum error correction becomes more hardware efficient when physical noise is strongly biased towards one error channel. Cat qubits realize such a bias by encoding information in two opposite coherent states of a superconducting oscillator, so that bit flips are exponentially suppressed with photon number while phase-flip rates increase only linearly. In Kerr-cat qubits, a driven double-well potential confines these states and enables fast coherent control, but excitations can induce interwell switching, limiting bit-flip times to milliseconds. Here we show that the nonlinear interaction generating the confinement can also cool these excitations. When an intra-well transition becomes resonant with a lossy readout mode, excitations are transferred out of the qubit and dissipated, as established by spectroscopy and relaxation measurements. We observe the predicted exponential scaling of Kerr-cat bit-flip times with photon number, reaching 450 s, over five orders of magnitude beyond previous demonstrations. Phase-flip rates remain consistent with intrinsic photon loss at operating points with seconds-long bit-flip times. We further demonstrate fast Z gates without measurable degradation of bit-flip protection and single-shot readout with a bit-flip probability below $10^{-6}$ per measurement. Autonomous cooling thus brings minutes-long bit-flip protection to Kerr-cat qubits while retaining fast coherent control, without additional cooling drives or circuit elements.
n97de3d45d1e6: Magnetic field detection is of great significance in modern fields such as medical diagnostics, geological exploration, inertial navigation, and space physics. We have previously investigated the expansion dynamics of a spin-orbit-coupled Bose-Einstein condensate. Building on these results, here we propose a scheme for magnetic-field-gradient detection by establishing a quantitative relationship between the condensate's rotational deflection angle and the magnetic-field gradient. In this work, we present the parameter dependence of this scheme and perform a systematic optimization. We introduce a Bayesian optimization algorithm to automatically and efficiently search for the optimal combination of key parameters, thereby significantly enhancing the sensitivity of the magnetic field gradient measurement. The results show that the optimized gradiometer improves the sensitivity by a factor of five. This work not only provides a new approach for magnetic field gradient measurement but also serves as a reference for machine learning-empowered quantum precision measurement.
n23c6a4b2afb2: Exploring interactions between quantum emitters and guided photons, waveguide quantum electrodynamics (wQED) offers a versatile platform for quantum simulation and quantum interconnect. To simplify the quantized light-matter interactions, a linearized dispersion approximation (LDA) was widely used in wQED under the conditions of weak coupling and narrow photonic bandwidth. However, a growing number of strong-coupling wQED experiments have called the validity of LDA into question. Here, by investigating giant atoms coupled to a semi-infinite waveguide, we propose a principle to judge the validity of LDA. We find that the decoherence of the atoms exhibits rich dynamical behaviors determined by different numbers of bound states in and out of the continuum (BICs and BOCs) formed in the energy spectrum of the total atom-photon system. Based on this, we show that despite the LDA can partially preserve some of BICs, it completely erases BOCs. This causes the dominant role of LDA in the atomic dynamics to break down. Providing a physical insight into the validity of LDA, our results lay a firm foundation for exploring fundamental physics and its application frontier in strong-coupling wQED platforms.
n3c0d4a68022f: In the graph collision problem, the task is to decide whether a known graph on $n$ vertices contains an edge with both endpoints marked, given query access to the input bits specifying the marked vertices. We first refute the conjectured $Ω(n^{2/3})$ query lower bound with a bounded error quantum algorithm using $\widetilde O(n^{92/139})$ queries. We then refine this approach to obtain a $\widetilde O(n^{11/17})$ query algorithm. We also obtain a $\widetilde O((nq)^{11/17})$ query bound for all (partial) Boolean output functions with positive certificate complexity at most 2 and alphabet size $q$, contrasting a known $Ω(n^{2/3})$ lower bound for such problems with large alphabet sizes. We complement these algorithms with an $Ω(\sqrt{n\log n})$ quantum query lower bound for graph collision, exceeding the $O(\sqrt n)$ certificate complexity barrier for the positive adversary method.
na4c0efe819e7: We study the one- and two-boson energy subspaces of finite open Bose--Hubbard chains with Fibonacci-modulated hopping and zero on-site potential. Their spectra exhibit a hierarchy of bands and gaps, and a critical zero-energy mode for odd lengths, in agreement with prior research. For the singe-excitation subspace we find two families of length-invariant finite-energy states localized at the left cluster boundary. For the two-boson subspace, we report both doublon and separated-pair excitations in the form of Tamm/Shockley states localized near either end. In particular, the right-edge doublon states occur across all Fibonacci generations whereas the left-side states appear every second generation. We check numerically that the second-order perturbation theory accounts well for the structure of the spectrum and the edge states in the doublon subspace in the strong-coupling regime. The results are useful for future explorations of many-body physics beyond numerical tractability, specifically using near-term Josephson quantum simulators.
n6b24644003f6: We discuss the relationship between quantum Hamiltonian embeddings (arXiv:2610.26833) and prior developments in Quantum Cognition Machine Learning (QCML), including QCML's earlier implementation on IBM quantum hardware. We consider the novelty claims and the computational role of encoding an entire dataset in a single ground state.
nf9e8119b6c8a: High-throughput inference remains a central challenge for equivariant machine-learned interatomic potentials. Here we introduce FACTO, an atom-centered equivariant architecture that confines evolving learned state and dense channel mixing to atoms, expressing neighbor interactions as fully fusible reductions. We complement this design with custom register-accumulated aggregation kernels and tensor-core FP32 emulation, accelerating inference while retaining FP32-level energy conservation under emulated arithmetic in molecular dynamics. Comprehensive evaluations on Matbench Discovery, MLIP Arena and MatCalc demonstrate high throughput alongside strong predictive accuracy and physical reliability. On Matbench Discovery, the four FACTO-OAM variants show top-tier performance by overall rank sum among 46 models with complete scores, advancing the accuracy-throughput Pareto frontier. On MLIP Arena, FACTO achieves state- of-the-art stability under extreme heating and compression, alongside high fidelity in hydrogen combustion. On MatCalc, FACTO outperforms the compared baselines in structural and elastic predictions while retaining competitive accuracy for energetic and thermal properties.
n33dbdda6146f: Battery degradation remains a central challenge in the development and broad application of sustainable energy technologies. Accurate degradation prediction is challenging, as battery aging emerges from complex and heterogeneous interactions among cycling behavior, operating conditions, and cell chemistry. Existing machine-learning approaches typically focus on deterministic end-of-life predictions or modeling degradation curves within fixed chemistry settings, leaving probabilistic state of health (SOH) trajectory modeling across heterogeneous chemistries underexplored. We introduce FlowBatt, a use-inspired conditional generative framework that adapts flow matching with a diffusion transformer (DiT) backbone to battery degradation trajectory modeling. FlowBatt models full SOH trajectories as probabilistic degradation processes conditioned on early-cycle capacity data. To strengthen this conditioning pathway, we use explainable AI analysis to diagnose and improve the encoder that maps early-cycle capacity matrices into conditioning vectors. We evaluate FlowBatt on five public benchmark settings spanning diverse chemistries and aging conditions, comparing it with supervised and diffusion-based trajectory models as well as established baselines for remaining useful life (RUL) prediction under shared data splits. FlowBatt achieves the best trajectory-wise SOH prediction performance on all five datasets, with errors below 2.5%, and delivers competitive RUL prediction performance. By generating multiple plausible trajectories, FlowBatt provides empirical prediction intervals for battery degradation modeling. These results indicate that flow-matching-based trajectory modeling is a promising framework for probabilistic battery health prediction.
nf1f1dcc9a117: We present a fully GPU-native framework for machine learning/molecular mechanics (ML/MM) enhanced sampling simulations with electrostatic embedding, demonstrated on an enzymatic reaction. The framework combines a JAX port of the pretrained MACE-POLAR-1-M model, an electrostatic embedding scheme compatible with the MACE-POLAR architecture, and integration with JAX-MD and PLUMED-JAX for end-to-end compiled enhanced sampling. The implementation is developed using GPT-6.1-Sol within Codex, with reasoning effort set to high. Using replica exchange umbrella sampling, we calculate the free energy profile of nucleophilic substitution in haloalkane dehalogenase in approximately 200 H100 GPU hours, treating the entire protein and reactants with MACE-POLAR-1-M-JAX and most of the solvent with molecular mechanics.
n106723caee14: Foundation machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) offer one model for many chemistries, but their deep, globally coupled architectures do not fit the spatial decomposition that scales classical and short-ranged MLIPs. We present pair_style uma, a LAMMPS pair style that evaluates the Universal Model for Atoms (UMA) through LibTorch on NVIDIA and Intel GPUs from a single source tree. It reimplements FairChem's edge-sharded graph parallelism in C++ over exported TorchScript modules, with one MPI rank per device, NCCL or oneCCL collectives, and the whole energy and force path in double precision. The strain-gradient virial is carried through the exported modules and the cross-device reductions, so that fix npt runs on both vendors' hardware. We measure NPT capacity and cost on one 4xA100-40GB node, one 8xH200 node, and one 12-tile Intel node, and on up to 32 Intel nodes. Without activation checkpointing, one node holds NaCl cells of about 8,000 atoms (A100, 0.21 ns/day), 22,000 atoms (Intel, 0.10 ns/day), and 47,000 atoms (H200, 0.16 ns/day). Graph parallelism raises the capacity of a single device by 8.0x on H200 and 4.6x on A100. Across nodes, capacity grows to about 779,000 atoms on 32 Intel nodes, with a slower speed at 0.007 ns/day. On H200 and A100, a FLOP count of FairChem's graph-parallel predictor gives lower bounds of 31% and 51% of FP64 peak. From one omat checkpoint and with no refit, nine 100 ps NPT heating ramps (NaCl, equiatomic Pt-Ru, and equiatomic (HfNbTaTiZr)N, on all three node types) ran to completion.
n8e9ab70a92a7: A general density functional theory based relativistic theory for paramagnetic NMR (pNMR) shifts, EPR g-tensors and hyperfine coupling tensors as well as magnetizabilities is derived. The formulation uses spin--orbit exact two-component (X2C) theory, gauge-including atomic orbitals, and generalized complex Kohn--Sham response equations with all ingredients being implemented analytically with the help of Goldstone modes and an orientation-constrained shielding. Additionally, we describe a two-component augmented Roothaan--Hall (ARH) solver for robust and stable convergence, which ensures that both a stationary point and a minimum are found. This is crucial for the convergence of the response equations for properties of paramagnetic systems. The extension of common population analyses for the two-component theory to aid in the interpretation of the spectra is further described. Using these new techniques, we are able to analyze the success and failure of density functional theory for relativistic open-shell systems including actinide complexes.
n9817e1f2c22c: Machine-learned interatomic potentials have greatly expanded the reach of molecular dynamics simulations, but complex chemical environments often require explicit treatment of long-range electronic response, including charge transfer and polarization. Physics-based flexible-charge models capture these effects but require global nonlinear charge equilibration at every time step to obtain Born-Oppenheimer energies and forces. This process is computationally expensive and can lead to instabilities unless tightly converged. Here, we introduce a shadow molecular dynamics framework for flexible-charge models with arbitrary local nonlinearities and long-range multipolar electrostatics. We replace the exact Born-Oppenheimer potential with a nearby shadow potential obtained by exactly equilibrating a partially linearized electronic energy functional. This provides conservative forces and reduces the global nonlinear equilibration to a quasi-diagonal linear problem that can be solved directly at low cost. Auxiliary dynamical electronic degrees of freedom, propagated through an extended-Lagrangian dynamics, capture the long-range electronic response and define the reference state for the linearization of the energy functional. GPU-accelerated simulations with over 100,000 atoms demonstrate that the shadow potential closely follows the tightly converged Born-Oppenheimer surface, while maintaining long-term stability at a computational cost approaching that of a fixed-charge model. These advances establish an efficient and broadly applicable framework for machine-learned interatomic potentials that explicitly incorporate long-range electrostatic interactions and environment-dependent electronic response.
n36738ddce1c1: Determining the representative volume element is essential for establishing statistically meaningful microstructure-property relationships. Conventional approaches rely on the convergence of selected geometric descriptors, which may yield different estimates of the representative volume. Here, we propose a topology-based framework for assessing the representative scale of a nickel-yttria-stabilized zirconia solid oxide cell anode reconstructed using plasma focused ion beam-scanning electron microscopy (121.8 um x 83.97 um x 45.99 um). Persistent homology was used to characterize the pore network, and normalized persistence images of subvolumes were compared with those of the largest available reference volume using the L1 distance. This provides a continuous measure of topological similarity across observation scales, rather than defining representativeness through a single convergence threshold. The topological distance decreases with increasing volume and is described by empirical exponential models over the investigated range (R2 in [0.972, 0.983]). Comparison with porosity and specific surface area highlights differences in the scale-dependent behavior of geometric and topological descriptors. The framework was also tested on three independent synthetic realizations, demonstrating its potential for quantitative assessment of topological similarity in porous microstructures.
nd41008265f97: Predictive COSMO-RS-based electrolyte models such as COSMO-RS-ES describe electrolyte solutions from quantum-chemical information, but treat the liquid as incompressible and give no access to densities or pressure effects. This work presents openCOSMO-RS-ES-Phi, to our knowledge the first open-source implementation of a predictive electrolyte equation of state based on openCOSMO-RS. It combines the COSMO-RS-based equation of state openCOSMO-RS-Phi with the ion interaction energies and the long-range term of COSMO-RS-ES, which is first refitted on the same simplified short range. With this refit, a dielectric decrement improves the mean ionic activity coefficients (MIAC), whereas a Born term counts the solvation of the ions a second time and is therefore left out. The equation of state then adds only volume, dispersion and temperature parameters of the ions, fitted to aqueous MIAC and densities. openCOSMO-RS-ES-Phi reproduces COSMO-RS-ES in dilute aqueous solutions, improves on it in concentrated ones and also yields solution densities. Extrapolating from aqueous systems, it predicts the MIAC in water + cosolvent mixtures as accurately as the fitted COSMO-RS-ES, as well as the MIAC and bubble points of a benchmark database of water-alcohol-salt systems. Salting-out of organic components is not described as accurately, and salts come out too soluble in organic solvents. Overall, the interaction model developed for COSMO-RS-ES carries over to a large extent to an equation of state, which makes openCOSMO-RS-ES-Phi a sound base model for further development, with ion transfer between solvents as a clear target for fitting to non-aqueous data.
n56efdc1ed6a8: Metalloprotein docking requires a ligand pose to satisfy both global pocket fit and the identity and geometry of metal-coordinating atoms. General-purpose diffusion docking models do not explicitly condition generation on externally specified complete ligand donor sets, and their predicted poses can exhibit incorrect metal-donor relationships. Metal-aware models address coordination during training and generation; here we ask whether external donor information can correct already-trained general-purpose models without retraining. We propose Complete-Identity Contract Guidance (CICG), which applies a supplied complete donor set through translation, rotation, and torsion updates, and Historical Contract Transfer (HCT), which supplies donor identities from earlier complexes at compatible receptor sites. We compare HCT with trajectory-local controls retaining the historical donor count with or without elemental composition. On 86 assessable HCT-covered queries, HCT-guided CICG increases frozen-confidence-selected joint success from 21.5% to 36.6% on SurfDock and from 25.0% to 34.9% on DiffDock-L. The joint criterion requires correct global ligand placement, complete native donor recovery, coordination geometry, preserved stereochemistry, and absence of fatal receptor clashes. Composition-matched guidance reaches 33.14% and 34.30%, leaving the additional benefit of fixed historical membership unresolved. Our results therefore support donor-set guidance as a conditional correction for frozen docking models, while identifying donor-source reliability and physical-quality preservation as the main barriers to broader use.
n7e7adaef083e: The coupling between plasmon resonances of metal nanostructures and electronic excitations of molecular/semiconductor systems is important in a number of applications, including surface enhanced spectroscopy, hot-electron catalysis, plasmon-induced resonance energy transfer and the creation of hybrid light-matter states. The past several decades has seen a large number of experimental studies of these effects, as well as the development of theory to explain the results. In this Perspectives article we use classical electromagnetic (EM) simulations to examine how the localized surface plasmon resonances (LSPRs) of metal nanoparticles and propagating surface plasmon polaritons (SPPs) in extended metal nanostructures (wires/plates/films) are affected by interactions with a molecular/semiconductor system. The classical EM simulations are complemented by a quantum model for plasmon-exciton coupling based on the macroscopic quantum electrodynamics (MQED) framework, along with Holstein vibrations. The goals are to show how LSPR spectra and SPP dispersion curves/attenuation constants changes as the strength of the molecular/semiconductor electronic transition increases and the system evolves from an energy transfer limit to strong coupling, and to provide an understanding of the decay processes from both classical EM and MQED perspectives.
nc1748ee99896: Water electrolysis is a promising technology for sustainable hydrogen (H$_2$) production. However, gas bubble formation significantly degrades the electrochemical surface area ($A_{\rm EC}$) and the electrocatalytic activity of microstructured electrodes in water electrolyzer cells. Existing theoretical models fail to connect computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and electrochemistry to analyze how bubble dynamics affect the performance of gas-evolving microstructured electrodes. This work develops a multiphysics-based theoretical model that couples two-phase CFD with Butler-Volmer and Faradaic kinetics, incorporating exchange current density, cell current, gravitational acceleration, surface tension, and fluid properties such as density and viscosity. The model quantifies essential electrochemical parameters, such as the enhancement in $A_{\rm EC}$ and the overpotential ($η$), which deviate by less than 7\% and 15\%, respectively, from the experimental results. Evaluations of the fabricated microstructured electrodes using polarization curves, cyclic voltammetry, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, and linear polarization resistance techniques demonstrate reduced $η$ by 2.49--21.39\% and 9.55--24.32\% for oxygen (O$_2$) and H$_2$ evolution, respectively. Furthermore, the model reveals the interplay between enhanced geometric surface area and bubble-transport limitations, facilitating the optimization and analysis of structural parameters. These findings establish a physics-informed roadmap for designing optimal, robust, and industry-scalable microstructured electrodes for efficient H$_2$ generation via water electrolysis.
nde555943fb67: Thermodynamic control seeks to realize desired functions at minimal thermodynamic cost, yet existing frameworks remain largely confined to slow driving regimes or state-to-state transport. Here we establish a thermodynamic optimal-control theory for Markov jump processes (MJPs) and chemical reaction networks (CRNs) that accommodates objectives over both states and reaction fluxes beyond slow-driving limit. By deriving the thermodynamic Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman equation, we demonstrate that the optimal dynamics take the form of a perturbed generalized-gradient flow driven by the value function. A convex representation of the entropy-production rate via generalized means identifies its Legendre--Fenchel dual as the dissipation function. The resulting dynamics shares the thermodynamic structure of CRNs and admits an information-geometric characterization. We further derive a thermodynamic Pontryagin equation by recasting the control problem in terms of thermodynamic forces, providing a complementary description of optimal trajectories and clarifying connections to thermodynamic optimal transport. Our results establish a thermodynamic and geometric foundation for controlling MJPs and CRNs beyond mere transport, opening avenues for optimizing biological processes and finite-time thermodynamic operations in far-from-equilibrium regimes.
n14bdcb0dc579: An electrochemical-thermal model of the 4680 cylindrical cell is presented: a Doyle-Fuller-Newman model of the electrode stack coupled to a two-node thermal balance of the roll and the can (a thermal DFN, TDFN), solved by an implicit finite-volume scheme. Two cells are parameterised from teardown geometry and open literature, with every value tagged by provenance: the Tesla NMC811/graphite tabless cell and the BYD FC4680 LiFePO4 multi-tab cell. The reaction heat is evaluated at the open-circuit potential of the particle-mean concentration, which restores the heat of mixing. Both sets are calibrated in the same way, with the test fixture identified from the measurement alone. Against the 1C and 2C charge test of Ank et al., the calibrated NMC set follows the mean can temperature within 0.52 and 1.46 K, with a contact heat of 0.94 mOhm matching the authors' estimate for their holder. For the LFP cell, 1C and 2C discharges to 2.0 V were measured on the authors' bench; the fixture conductance (0.337 W/K) follows from the energy balance and the heat capacity (277 J/K) from the cooling. With the end-of-lithiation drop of LiFePO4 restored in the cathode open-circuit potential, the calibrated set follows the can temperature within 0.44 K (1C) and 0.76 K (2C), reproduces the peaks and the relaxation after cut-off. What remains is what a single can node and a single representative particle do not describe: the axial gradient of the NMC can under contact heating, and a gradual decline of the LFP voltage before the knee at 2C, which points to the distribution of particle states in the electrode. The parameter sets (BPX, CSV) and the bench data are openly available.
neacd05d8c055: Diffusion models are often inaccurate in critical, data-sparse regions of the target distribution. Sampling from restrained distributions, biased distributions used in classical enhanced sampling to concentrate data near chosen configurations, can control where training data are collected but biases the learned distribution. We establish that this bias cancels exactly when forward noising from restrained data is conditioned on the restrained configuration at an appropriately chosen intermediate time. This allows a pretrained model fine-tuned on restrained data to achieve high accuracy in any chosen region of the target distribution, regardless of its probability, using standard denoising or flow matching objectives without importance weights. When no target data are available, Gibbs sampling enables inference from a model trained exclusively on restrained data.
n59d5d27f3915: Understanding how confinement alters the transport of charged molecules is central to the advancement of separation, energy, and sensing technologies. Polyamines are small, linear molecules with ionizable groups, making them an ideal model for investigating charge transport in confinement beyond monatomic ions. Using all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, we investigate how molecular length, net charge, and charge placement affect the electrophoretic transport of polyamines through single-walled carbon nanotubes (CNTs). We find that nanometer-scale confinement reverses the mobility ordering observed in free solution -- in a CNT of radius 0.68 nm, spermine (q = +4) travels more slowly than ethylamine (q = +1), contrasting with the expected scaling of mobility with valence in bulk. Further, we find that mobility decreases faster than the inverse of valence, though molecular size and length vary alongside this trend. Comparisons of doubly protonated spermidine microspecies reveal the additional influence of charge placement at fixed net valence. Upon moving one proton of dicationic spermidine from the central to a terminal nitrogen, the mobility is increased by 42%. We analyze hydration structure and solute-solvent association, identifying local-solvation differences between protonation topologies that accompany these distinct transport responses under confinement. These results suggest that neutral CNTs could support valence-selective nanofluidic transport, with additional sensitivity to molecular structure and protonation topology.
n91df90899493: In a crowded extracellular environment, viruses and nanoparticles must reach the cell membrane within a few nanometers before the first ligand-receptor bond can form. Crowders generate an entropic depletion attraction, yet continuum models usually assume contact is already established or treat the approach deterministically. We formulate a thermodynamically consistent stochastic theory for this pre-contact stage. The sphere-plane depletion geometry uses the exact Asakur-Oosawa spherical-cap overlap, rather than a fitted cap, with either ideal van 't Hoff or pressure-only Carnahan-Starling osmotic pressure. A spatially varying near-wall mobility introduces a noise-induced drift that is essential for thermodynamic consistency and is often omitted. The first specific reaction is modeled by a Robin radiation boundary; the outer boundary is reflecting or absorbing. Three first-passage problems are solved analytically by quadrature: the mean reaction time, the reaction-before-escape probability, and the conditional success time, the last encoded by a Doob transform that exposes the selection bias of conditioning on capture. The theory separates thermodynamic inputs from conditional parameters and reveals a reaction-limited to diffusion-limited crossover controlled by the local Damköhler number. For typical virus and nanoparticle parameters, the depletion well reaches $2$-$6\,k_{\rm B}T$, capture times are $0.1$-$1\,{\rm ms}$, and the conditional success time is measurably shorter than the unconditional mean. Finite-volume and Chebyshev schemes reproduce the analytic results within their discretization errors and satisfy the radiation-boundary mass balance. This provides a quantitative theoretical framework for crowding-assisted capture prior to membrane wrapping and a reference for comparing crowding, near-wall mobility, and surface reactivity in endocytosis.
n233b5f9aa7b5: We develop a density-functional theory for the Pauli-Fierz Hamiltonian of nonrelativistic quantum electrodynamics in the spirit of the convex-analytic formulation of Lieb. We consider finitely many electrons, subject to external scalar and vector potentials, coupled to the full continuum of massless transverse photons with an ultraviolet cutoff. The natural basic variables are the standard electron density and a combined current density, the sum of the paramagnetic current density and a field-induced current density generated by the quantized vector potential. We prove representability results for these density-current pairs and show that the mixed-state constrained-search functional attains its infimum and coincides with the Lieb functional obtained by convex conjugation. Since arbitrarily soft photons purify mixed states at a negligible energy cost without changing their density and combined current density, the pure-state Levy-Lieb functional equals the Lieb functional and is therefore convex, even though its infimum need not be attained. In addition, we establish the zero-coupling limit, which recovers the mixed-state Vignale-Rasolt functional of current-density-functional theory. Finally, we consider the long-wavelength (dipole) limit and show that the limiting functional can be written as a constrained search for the well-known length-gauge dipole Hamiltonian.
nf2a6ef847530: Onsager's variational principle (OVP) constructs dissipative dynamics from free energy, dissipation, and input power, but deterministic rate laws alone do not identify fluctuations or chemical fuel consumption. We examine these distinctions for nonlinear reaction kinetics in active matter. Comparing Gaussian diffusion and Poisson reaction events clarifies when statistical fluctuations match a physical Rayleighian: the reaction dissipation potential must be consistent with counting statistics, local detailed balance links rate bias to chemical affinity, and kinetic scales remain constitutive inputs. Under these conditions, the normalized Rayleighian excess gives the leading rate-fluctuation cost in the frozen-state, many-event regime. Three models illustrate the consequences. Spatially uniform reactions exhibit protocol-dependent nonreciprocal response compatible with fixed-state OVP; different Rayleighian representations can select the same rate without specifying the same fluctuations. In an active emulsion, a finite fuel pool accounts for free-energy transfer and dissolution of a chemically maintained domain after replenishment stops. In a membrane-cytosol model, distinct reaction-channel realizations yield identical protein-density trajectories but different chemical input power. Under a separate kinetic assumption, an exact total-density equation still requires an initial rate and does not determine chemical work or fluctuations. These results clarify the physical and statistical inputs required for constructing reaction-transport models and interpreting their fluctuations.
n858ba4d4ad90: After a particle forms its first receptor--ligand bond near a cell membrane, stable attachment often requires a threshold number of additional bonds. This paper develops a biophysical kinetic theory of this post-capture stage. The bond-number dynamics are modeled as a finite birth--death chain on $n=0,1,\dots,m$, where $0$ is loss of the initial bond and $m$ is the stabilization threshold. The mesoscopic rates $λ_n$ and $μ_n$ encode the local energy landscape, accessible receptor--ligand pairs, steric and orientational constraints, and cooperative interactions within the growing cluster. The probability of reaching the threshold before losing the first bond is derived in closed form for general rates and, in the constant-ratio case, reduces to a geometric series controlled by the free-energy bias $ρ_n=μ_n/λ_n$. The mean time to failure or stabilization follows from a tridiagonal backward equation. Conditioning on successful attachment is treated as a trajectory-selection effect: the conditioned chain is a Doob $h$-transform whose dissociation rate at $n=1$ vanishes, because successful trajectories cannot lose the first bond early. A minimal interface between the spatial first-capture probability and the bond-number chain is formulated, together with the conditions under which the stable capture probability factorizes into their product. The analysis shows that hitting probabilities constrain only the rate ratios, whereas the absolute rate scale requires time-resolved or dwell-time data. The threshold $m$ is a model-defined stabilization criterion, not a directly measured ligand count. The rates and threshold are effective parameters specified independently or inferred from kinetic data. The theory provides a quantitative framework for interpreting attachment probabilities, lifetimes, and the transition from first bond formation to stable multivalent adhesion.
ne79e0f6eaf0d: We propose a hierarchical scale-bridging construction for building first principles electronic structure models of extended molecular aggregates with disorder, and its practical realization in exciton systems. The general construction, referred here as to the encapsulation, is based on a recursive operator-valued hierarchy cast in a dual graph-theoretic (discrete) and configuration-space (continuous) structure, in which variables associated with a coarser level parameterize operators governing the degrees of freedom at the next finer level in a graph-covariant, geometry-preserving fashion. In an exemplary application of this scheme, aggregate-level ground- and excited-state operators are constructed through a many-body expansion (MBE), with matrix elements evaluated in a basis comprising the aggregate ground state and local Frenkel excitations. The required monomer and dimer building blocks are obtained from DFT and TDDFT calculations, yielding aggregate-level 1-particle transition density matrices as well as Hamiltonian, dipole moment and other operators that can be evaluated at the level of the building blocks. Starting from structural models obtained from experiment or molecular dynamics, this approach generates aggregate-level operators in a bottom-up fashion without fitting parameters to spectroscopic data or performing calculations on larger system cutouts. A numerical demonstration is given for an excitonic manifold in crystalline quaterthiophene. In particular, through its intrinsic configuration-dependence encoded in the encapsulations, it will provide a bridge between static electronic structure calculations for realistic, structurally disordered aggregates and quantum or quantum-classical simulations of exciton-vibrational dynamics.
nd82ca71357ac: Accurate measurement of reduced density matrices (RDMs) is central to quantum simulations of many-fermion systems, but the required measurement resources remain a significant challenge. Constrained shadow tomography (CST) combines randomized measurements with $N$-representability conditions to reconstruct physically valid RDMs from limited measurement data. Here we improve CST by orthogonalizing the measurement constraints and using the resulting singular values to determine the relative weight of each independent measurement direction according to how strongly it is sampled by the quantum computer. These optimally weighted constraints are incorporated into the semidefinite program through a least-squares objective implemented with a Schur-complement relaxation. We demonstrate the approach for hydrogen chains on a quantum simulator and for azobenzene on a quantum processor. In both cases, optimally weighted CST systematically improves the accuracy of the reconstructed 2-RDM without increasing the measurement budget, providing a more measurement-efficient approach to partial tomography for quantum simulations of correlated fermions.
n371d2fe7e1e2: We present PLUMED-JAX, an AI-assisted adaptation of selected PLUMED collective variables, umbrella sampling, and metadynamics for JAX-based atomistic simulations, developed using gpt-6.1-sol with reasoning effort set to high within the Codex harness. Integration with JAX-MD supports compiled molecular dynamics, batched replicas, walkers sharing a bias, and execution across multiple graphics processing units. We validate the framework against PLUMED and exact free energy benchmarks, and demonstrate applications to butane, silicon crystallization, and lithium transport, with severalfold improvements in computational throughput for both classical forcefields and machine learning interatomic potentials.
n798a95a282ca: Liquid-phase peptide synthesis (LPPS) offers a scalable route to peptide manufacturing, but route development still depends on empirical solvent screens because each protected intermediate must be soluble for reaction and recoverable for purification. The protecting groups, terminal modifications, and noncanonical residues that govern this behaviour are poorly represented in existing peptide property benchmarks, limiting the ability to develop and rigorously evaluate molecular representation models for LPPS-relevant prediction tasks. We introduce PeptSol, an open benchmark of 1388 hand-curated protected-peptide solubility measurements with chemistry-aware splits. The measurements span only 84 parent sequences and 101 protected structures, and 92.5% come from a single historical programme. Across seven frozen molecular encoders, the best macro-F1 is 0.843 on binary solubility for the historical subset under a peptide-held-out split; the harder three-class ordinal task reaches 0.614 in that cell. No foundation model consistently outperforms a baseline combining chemical fingerprints with explicit molecular descriptors, and model rankings vary across prediction tasks and data splits. The dataset, evaluation protocol, and baselines establish a standard for measuring progress on molecular representations for synthesis-aware peptide developability.
n046680d7af45: Weakly correlated electronic structures are predominant among molecules, and are routinely solved with heuristic classical methods such as the ``gold standard'' CCSD(T) coupled cluster model, incurring a formal time complexity $O(n^7)$ in the number of molecular orbitals and with no guarantee of energy error $\varepsilon$ at or below chemical accuracy. In this work, a quantum algorithm is presented for ground state energy estimation of weakly correlated molecules using Trotterized time evolution, with an end-to-end quantum operations cost that scales as $\tilde{O}(n^{4.8}/\varepsilon^2)$ in the limit of high-order product formulae when run as a low-depth, shot-noise limited algorithm, or $\tilde{O}(n^{4.8} + n^{3.8}/\varepsilon)$ when scaling the simulation time $T\propto 1/\varepsilon$. The algorithm combines adiabatic state preparation using a smoothed Gevrey schedule with eigenstate filtering via quantum prolate diagonalization (QPD). Both steps of the algorithm rely on a size-independent spectral gap assumption, which is validated by numerical studies on alanine chains with up to 64 monomers. We benchmark the performance of our eigenstate filtering algorithm on a set of 28 molecules to compare our approach against prior phase estimation algorithms, finding that QPD achieves state-of-the-art cost tradeoffs for $\varepsilon$-accurate results. Physical quantum resource estimates are obtained for running Trotter step circuits with up to 40 spin-orbitals, providing a clear path for scaling up quantum simulation of chemistry on early fault-tolerant hardware.
nf26ffe598bc6: We introduce ROSE, a deep-learning exchange--correlation energy functional built from the occupied-state density matrix. On GMTKN55 and on additional external benchmarks considered in this work, ROSE improves over modern neural network functionals trained under matched protocols and is on average more accurate than, or on par with, most hybrid and range-separated hybrid functionals considered here. On the experimental benchmarks considered here it has leading accuracy across hybrids, range separated hybrids, and neural functionals. These results motivate nonlocal density-matrix representations as a route to systematic improvement of learned XC functionals with low computational cost.
n2f4be1b9d617: Within a hybrid quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics approach a small region of a large atomistic system is described quantum mechanically, while the rest of the system is represented by a classical force field. Despite this, the computational cost of the quantum calculation severely limits the accessible simulation and sampling time. Replacing the quantum calculation with a machine learning interatomic potential (MLIP) trained on quantum reference data can greatly increase the accessible simulation time. However, the accuracy and efficiency strongly depend on the specific way in which the MLIP incorporates information about the classical (electrostatic) environment. Here, we demonstrate that existing strategies based purely on features derived from an external electric field fail to distinguish certain environments, ultimately limiting their accuracy. As a solution, we propose an extension to the equivariant TensorNet architecture that mitigates this shortcoming by incorporating classical atoms close to the quantum region into the message-passing scheme, combined with features derived from the electric field for describing the environment farther away. We show that this combination achieves higher accuracy than either approach alone.
nc1920020c0bb: Nonequilibrium polariton condensation is a macroscopic quantum phenomenon in which overwhelming population accumulation is observed at the band edge of the lower polariton (LP) dispersion curve under incoherent material pumping. As a promising route toward nonequilibrium Bose--Einstein condensates, its description, however, remains predominantly limited to models with phenomenological material parameters. Herein, a fully atomistic description of vibrational polariton condensation is developed by employing mesoscale cavity molecular dynamics simulations, a method which self-consistently propagates classical electromagnetic dynamics coupled to realistic molecules in a multimode Fabry--Pérot cavity. Under continuous-wave pumping, a lower polariton condensate forms when the infrared cavity is coupled to harmonic, homogeneously broadened molecular vibrations, such as the bending modes of liquid CO2 and CS2, whereas anharmonic stretching modes and liquids with fast intramolecular relaxation hardly condense. The role of libration-bending coupling for facilitating the LP condensation is further discussed. GPU-accelerated mesoscale simulations involving approximately 50 million atoms additionally provide direct two-dimensional real-space imaging of fluid-like polariton patterns during the condensation formation. Overall, this study provides key design insights into vibrational polariton condensation as a novel approach for controlling liquid-phase chemistry.
nc219ccd5a550: The exchange-correlation functional in Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory (TDDFT) is known to have dependence on past densities and initial states, and yet this memory-dependence is ignored in practical calculations which almost always use an adiabatic approximation. We discuss the dysfunction that arises due to this deficiency and point to therapies that go beyond the adiabatic approximation. Still, adiabatic TDDFT has had success in a wide range of systems for response properties and for fully non-equilibrium dynamics, and why this is so is only partially understood. This, together with the rigorous foundation of the exact theory and its favorable system-size scaling, provides tremendous impetus for continuing to strive towards improved approximations to the exact functionals, and a deeper understanding of the impact of approximations in applications.
n80e78467e183: The local pressure tensor of an inhomogeneous fluid is not unique. Two tangential profiles are in common use in planar simulations: the Irving-Kirkwood (IK) profile, which requires a dedicated pass over every pair of atoms for every slab, and the per-atom virial (PAV) profile, which molecular-dynamics codes produce at negligible cost and coincides with the Harasima contour. The two differ by the derivative of a pair quantity, P_T^IK - P_T^PAV = dQ/dz. We show that, for Lennard-Jones free-standing films, Q(z) can be predicted from the density profile and the bulk radial distribution function of the coexisting liquid: under the closure rho2(r1,r2) ~ rho(z1) rho(z2) g(r12), with a pair-local interpolation of g between its liquid and dilute limits, Q is a double integral of rho(z) against a kernel built from u'(r) g(r). The estimator P_T^IK,est = P_T^PAV + dQ/dz is tested against IK profiles measured on the same trajectories for 20 films (thicknesses 7-25 sigma, three cutoff radii, two temperatures): the root-mean-square residual is 0.001-0.002 epsilon/sigma^3, against 0.010-0.021 for the uncorrected profile, and Q, the amount that the contour choice transfers between the two interfaces of a film with non-equivalent surfaces, is recovered to within 0.6% of the surface tension. Applied to the normal component, the same closure removes 83-92% of the spurious structure of the per-atom zz profile, a test that needs no IK run. Its mixture form is validated on three two-component films with an adsorbate unequally distributed between their faces, where it resolves the tension of each face; a clean face recovers the tension of the pure film.
nf05fd9c6a093: Foundation models (FMs) learn reusable representations from large collections of unlabeled data. In chemistry the corresponding data mainly consists of molecular structures, which are abundant, whereas experimental measurements are scarce. Chemical FMs such as ChemBERTa and MoLFormer were therefore trained on diverse molecular structures to enable fine-tuning on small experimental datasets (less than 100 datapoints in most realistic scenarios) and subsequent property prediction. At the same time, general-purpose FMs such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 were trained on virtually all publicly available data, including knowledge of the humankind on molecular properties and laws governing them. Here we compare accuracies of chemical and general-purpose FMs on tasks from various areas of chemistry. Strikingly, general-purpose GPT-6 Astra outperforms the currently eligible chemical FMs on five physicochemical and quantum-chemical regression tasks when only 60 experimental datapoints are available. Only when provided 10x datapoints do the best chemical FMs reach performance of GPT-6 Astra: on 1,000 and 10,000 points they show performance on par with Astra on 60 and 1,000 points, respectively. Thus, counterintuitively, frontier general-purpose FMs are better suited for guiding chemical research in data-scarce areas than specialized chemical FMs, suggesting that learning relevant primitives (e.g. chemical structures) does not substitute training on relevant humankind knowledge.
